attacks.claim: For a [MessagePackObject] type whose member is a closed generic value type from a referenced assembly, the analyzer no longer throws IndexOutOfRangeException (AD0001).
For the same input the generator no longer throws (no CS8785) and a GeneratedMessagePackResolver is emitted.
Only struct<T> and record struct<T> from metadata change behaviour; struct, record struct, class<T> and record class<T> from metadata behave exactly as before.
attacks.scenario: A closed generic class (`class<T>`) from metadata with an unkeyed member also changes behavior, as it previously threw IndexOutOfRangeException (due to empty DeclaringSyntaxReferences) and now does not.
attacks.test_sketch: Create a `class MyGenericClass<T> { public int Unkeyed { get; set; } }` in a referenced assembly. Use `MyGenericClass<int>` in the main project and observe it no longer throws AD0001.

attacks.claim: No diagnostic that was reported before the change for a type declared in source is lost, moved or changed by the new constructor-level filter.
No safety-relevant diagnostic is silently dropped for types the user controls.
attacks.scenario: The user controls a referenced project, but that project does not have the MessagePack analyzer installed. Diagnostics for its types are silently dropped by the consuming project.
attacks.test_sketch: Create Project B with a generic type without keys, but do not install MessagePack.Analyzers in Project B. Create Project A referencing Project B and MessagePack.SourceGenerator. Build Project A. No diagnostics are reported, but the type is invalid.

attacks.claim: Diagnostics about the members of a closed generic type from a referenced assembly are reported by the assembly that defines it, so any problem must be fixed there.
attacks.scenario: The referenced assembly is a third-party library or a project without the MessagePack analyzer installed, meaning no diagnostics are reported anywhere.
attacks.test_sketch: Use a type from a third-party library (e.g., a generic struct from a NuGet package without MessagePack analyzers) that lacks `[Key]` attributes. Observe that no diagnostics are reported by either assembly.

attacks.claim: An unattributed public member of a type defined in a referenced assembly is reported by the project that defines that type.
attacks.scenario: The defining project does not have the MessagePack analyzer installed, so the unattributed member is never reported.
attacks.test_sketch: Create a class library without MessagePack analyzers, define a type with an unattributed public member, reference it in an app with MessagePack analyzers, and observe no diagnostic is reported.

attacks.claim: Dropping a diagnostic that has no location in the compilation is required because analyzers are not permitted to report against a location that does not exist.
attacks.scenario: Analyzers and source generators are permitted to report diagnostics that are not tied to a specific source location by using `Location.None`.
attacks.test_sketch: Call `context.ReportDiagnostic(Diagnostic.Create(Rule, Location.None))` in an analyzer or generator. It works perfectly fine and is a standard way to report compilation-wide issues.

attacks.claim: No live DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] indexing remains in TypeCollector.cs; the only remaining occurrence is commented out.
GetPropertyIdentifierLocation returns null only for properties that have no source declaration (metadata), so no source-declared property loses its diagnostic.
attacks.scenario: A property declared via a record primary constructor parameter has a source declaration but returns null because its syntax is `ParameterSyntax`, not `PropertyDeclarationSyntax`.
attacks.test_sketch: Define `public record MyRecord([Key(null)] string Prop);`. `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` will return `null` for `Prop` because the `as PropertyDeclarationSyntax` cast fails, causing the diagnostic to be dropped.
